questions.question: What happens when you 'squash' a commit in interactive rebase?
choices: The commit is deleted without any trace
The commit is combined into the previous commit, merging their messages
The commit is moved to the end of the history
questions.explanation: Squash combines the target commit's changes and message into the previous commit. The result is a single commit with a merged message like 'A + B'.

questions.question: Why must you deep copy commits before performing rebase operations?
choices: Deep copy is faster than shallow copy
To avoid mutating the original commit data during splice and merge operations
It doesn't matter — JavaScript arrays are passed by value
questions.explanation: Operations like splice modify the array in place. If you don't deep copy first, the original commits array gets corrupted, leading to unpredictable behavior.

questions.question: Why can't you squash the first commit in a sequence?
choices: The first commit is always protected by Git
There is no previous commit to combine it into
Squash requires at least two commits after the target
The first commit has no parent hash
questions.explanation: Squash merges a commit INTO the previous one. The first commit has no previous commit, so there's nothing to merge into.
